newsitem.title: UK: Britain agreed N.Irish march in June - newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Britain agreed N.Irish march in June - newspaper.

text.p: A British newspaper said on Tuesday a confidential government document showed authorities decided in early June on the route of the Sunday march in Northern Ireland which ignited an explosion of violence.

The Independent newspaper's account appeared to contradict Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam's statements that that she was seeking a compromise on the route of the Portadown march by the Protestant Orange Order up until early on Sunday morning.
The report seemed likely to cause more anger among Catholics and Irish nationalists who complain that the parade insulted their faith and trampled over their civil rights.

The holding of the march provoked a storm of Catholic rioting and cast a pall over Anglo-Irish attempts to forge a political settlement between the Catholic pro-Irish nationalist minority and pro-British Protestant majority.

Police chiefs and the British government said they decided to allow the Protestant Order to march through a Catholic area of Portadown after failing to secure a compromise in talks between the Orange Order and Catholic Portadown residents.
They also cited as reasons for the decision intelligence reports which suggested that pro-British Loyalist guerrillas would kill Catholics if the parade was banned or rerouted.

The Independent, however, said it had obtained a confidential document dated June 20 which showed that government ministers and police decided three weeks ago that a controlled parade along the Garvaghy road was "the least worst outcome".
By its account, the document made no mention of fears of attacks by Loyalists and was endorsed by John Steele, Director of Security at the British government's Northern Ireland office.

No one was immediately available for comment at the Northern Ireland Office. It made no statement when similar reports of the decision on Portadown were aired by the BBC and the independent Channel 4 television network on Monday night.

All three reports said that the authorites sought to get concessions from the Orange Order on the way it would conduct the march, such as a reduction in numbers, the absence of bands and the removal of regalia such as swords and flags.
It also hoped that the Order might be pressed to agree that it would enter talks with Catholic residents about next year's parade, something it has firmly refused to do.
The Orange Order accuses Catholic residents of being manipulated by Sinn Fein, political wing of Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas fighting British rule of Northern Ireland.
It is refusing to negotiate with Catholic residents over the route of two parades through Catholic areas next Saturday, when its annual "marching season" of street parades reaches a climax.
